#10345. Proton Pass is up to 60% off for Black Friday—and it does way more than just store your passwords

There’s a familiar interruption that comes with shopping online: you’ve found what you want, you’re ready to check out, and the store asks you to sign in. Was this the account with your usual password? Did you change it last time? Is it easier to reset it again?

Proton Pass is designed to take that friction out of your day. It creates strong, unique passwords, remembers them for you, and fills them in when you log in. But it also handles something a password alone can’t: keeping your real email address out of another retailer’s database.

For Black Friday, Proton Pass Plus and Pass Family are both 60% off their regular monthly pricing with a one-year subscription, while Proton Unlimited is 50% off. Pass Plus starts at $1.99 per month, billed annually, making this a good opportunity to get your passwords — and a few other important parts of your digital life — organized.

The problem with strong passwords isn’t understanding why you need them; it’s keeping track of a different one for every account.

Proton Pass does that work for you. When you sign up for a website, its password generator can create a strong password that’s completely unique. Save it in your vault, and Proton Pass can fill in your credentials when you return.

That’s useful whether you’re creating an account for a single purchase or signing into a service you use every day.

Unique passwords also help limit the fallout from a data breach. If a retailer exposes your login credentials, using a different password elsewhere means those same credentials won’t unlock your other accounts.

With unlimited logins and encrypted vaults that sync across devices, Proton Pass lets you keep those details together as you move between your phone and computer.

Proton Pass is available for practically every platform, from Chrome and Firefox on the web to native macOS, Windows, and Linux apps to, of course, iOS and Android. This makes it trivially easy to access your passwords, passkeys, and API credentials wherever you find yourself.

Black Friday shopping often leaves something behind long after the packages arrive: a steady stream of promotional emails from stores you barely remember visiting.

Proton Pass includes unlimited hide-my-email aliases, giving you an alternative to handing out your real address every time you create an account.

An alias is an extra email address that forwards messages to your normal inbox. You can give it to a shopping website and still receive your order confirmations and delivery updates, without sharing the underlying address you use for everything else.

If that alias starts receiving spam, you can switch it off. Your real email address stays the same, and you don’t have to update all your other accounts.

It’s a practical way to put some distance between your primary inbox and the websites you’re trying for the first time. A separate alias for each service also gives you more control: you can stop messages arriving through one address without disrupting the others.

Passwords are only part of what’s worth keeping in a secure, accessible place.

Proton Pass also stores notes, credit card details, and other confidential information in end-to-end encrypted vaults. That makes it useful for the small, everyday moments when you need something sensitive and don’t want to go looking for it.

When you’re booking a flight, saved passport details let you look up the information you need without digging through a drawer halfway through the reservation.

When you’re shopping online, saved card details mean you don’t have to leave the checkout page to find your wallet.

When you’re traveling, keeping a digital copy of an important document within reach gives you a convenient reference while you’re away from home. It doesn’t replace an original document where one is required, but it can save you from searching through scattered files and messages.

Pass Plus also includes a built-in two-factor authenticator, Dark Web Monitoring, and secure link and vault sharing. Those features give you more ways to manage access to your accounts and share sensitive information when you need to.

Pass Plus is the straightforward choice for one person who wants password generation, autofill, unlimited aliases, and secure storage.

Pass Family includes six Pass Plus accounts and a family admin panel. If several people in your household need a password manager, it’s worth considering rather than setting everyone up with separate subscriptions.

Proton Unlimited bundles Pass with Proton VPN, Proton Mail, Proton Drive, and more, including 500 GB of cloud storage. It’s the option to consider if you also want a VPN, encrypted email, and cloud storage alongside your password manager.

A password manager isn’t the most conspicuous Black Friday purchase, but it’s one you can put to work immediately: the next account you create, the next password you forget, or the next time a checkout asks for details you don’t have handy.

Proton’s offers are available to new users and include a 30-day money-back guarantee.

#10344. How to Migrate an Elementor Site to the WordPress Block Editor

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Elementor made your site easy to build. It may also be making it slow. Here's how to move a site onto the Block Editor without breaking URLs, losing content or dropping out of Google.

Page builders solved a real problem. Before the Block Editor matured, they were the easiest way to give clients drag-and-drop layouts. Many of those sites are still running today, and a lot of them are slow on phones.

The data backs that up. According to the HTTP Archive Core Web Vitals Technology Report for June 2026, 36.8% of Elementor sites pass Core Web Vitals on mobile. Sites built with the Block Editor pass 53.0% of the time. That's correlation, not proof, since hosting and setup matter too. But in my experience, it matches what happens when you remove the builder from a slow site.

My reason for migrating sites off Elementor is simple: **page builders make websites heavy. **Having said that, Elementor has improved a lot. Its performance settings, Flexbox Containers, and asset-loading options cut much of the bloat, and a carefully tuned Elementor site can pass Core Web Vitals. But tuning only goes so far. You’re still shipping the builder’s framework, wrapper markup and scripts, and every plugin or Elementor update is a chance for the speed to slip again.

For small business sites that don’t need drag-and-drop editing, rebuilding the same design on the WordPress Block Editor (Gutenberg) removes that weight at the source, without changing what the client sees.

This guide follows the order I use. It assumes you're comfortable with WordPress admin, WP-CLI and a staging site. If you need to set those up first, SitePoint's guide to the ultimate WordPress development environment covers the tooling.

Not every Elementor site needs to move. Migration makes sense when:

It's harder to justify when the site leans on Elementor Pro features you'd need to replace, such as complex popups, dynamic loops or WooCommerce templates. Those can all be rebuilt, but the job gets bigger fast.

You can't prove a migration worked without "before" numbers. Capture these on the live site first.

Crawl the site with a tool such as Screaming Frog, and export every indexable URL with its title, meta description, H1 and canonical tag. You can also pull published pages and posts with WP-CLI:

Run Google PageSpeed Insights, which uses Lighthouse for its lab scores, on the homepage and two or three key templates. Save the mobile lab scores and, if the site has enough traffic, the field data from real users.

Export the last three months of pages and queries from Google Search Console. That's what you'll compare against after launch.

Elementor stores each page's layout as JSON in the elementordata post meta field, and marks builder pages with elementoredit_mode. This command lists every page that uses the builder:

Then list everything else Elementor controls, which is easy to miss:

On the small business sites I've migrated, the inventory usually turns up more than the owner expects. The pages are the easy part. The surprises are saved templates nobody remembers creating, a popup still running on every page, add-on widgets from plugins that were installed once and forgotten, and contact forms that live inside Elementor Pro rather than a form plugin. Finding those before the rebuild saves a broken launch.

Work on a staging copy. Install a block theme, such as Twenty Twenty-Five or a lightweight starter theme, and move the Elementor global styles into theme.json. That way colors, fonts and spacing are defined once, instead of in every widget.

Copy the hex values and font names from Elementor's Site Settings so the new site matches the old one. Rebuild the header and footer as template parts in the Site Editor. If you'd rather write a theme yourself, SitePoint's series on building a WordPress theme from scratch covers the basics.

Most Elementor sites repeat the same few sections: a hero, a services grid, testimonials and a call to action. Build each one once as a block pattern, then reuse it on every page. Patterns are plain block markup, so you don't need React to write them, whatever you may have heard about React and WordPress development.

In a block theme, any PHP file in the /patterns folder with a header comment is registered automatically:

For page content, there's a useful shortcut. Elementor saves a plain HTML copy of each page into post_content. Open a page in the Block Editor, and the old content usually appears in a Classic block. Choose Convert to blocks, then delete the leftovers and rebuild the layout with your patterns. It keeps the copy and images, so you only redo the design.

The difference shows up in the page source. Here's typical front-end markup for a single heading on an Elementor page, using the older section and column layout:

Newer Elementor versions with Flexbox containers and the optimized markup settings trim some of those wrappers, but most older sites still carry all of them. Multiply that by every element on every page, and the weight adds up.

To speed up this step, I built a free Elementor to Gutenberg converter. Paste in a page's elementordata JSON from Step 2, and it returns block markup you can paste into the Block Editor's code editor. It handles headings, text, images, buttons, spacers, dividers and column layouts, and lists anything it can't convert, such as forms and popups, for you to rebuild by hand. It runs entirely in your browser, so the page data never leaves your computer.

The code is rarely what holds a migration up. Content is. Once clients see their site being rebuilt, many decide it's time to rewrite their pages too, and the project ends up waiting on copywriters and approvals. My fix is to separate the two: migrate the existing content as it is, launch, then update the copy afterwards. That keeps the speed and SEO gains on schedule, and it means any ranking change can be traced to either the migration or the new copy, not both at once.

This is the step that decides whether rankings hold.

To spot-check a redirect or a status code from the command line:

When staging matches the live site, deploy it. Then:

Leave the old elementordata meta in place for a few weeks, in case you need to roll back. Once you're confident, take a backup and remove it to shrink the database.

Run PageSpeed Insights again straight away for lab scores. Field data takes longer: the Chrome UX Report uses a rolling 28-day window, so give it a month before judging real-user results. Compare Search Console clicks for the same period before and after launch.

In my migrations, the biggest change is usually page weight and loading time, because the builder's CSS, JavaScript and wrapper markup are gone. What doesn't always improve is server response time. If the site is on slow shared hosting, the first byte still arrives late, and that needs a hosting fix, not a rebuild. Search traffic should hold steady if the URLs and metadata were protected. If it drops, the Step 5 crawl comparison is the first place to look.

Moving off Elementor isn't a one-click job, but it isn't a full redesign either. Record a baseline, inventory what the builder controls, rebuild with patterns, and protect every URL. Most of the speed gain comes from removing code the site never needed. For what to tackle after that, see these practical web performance techniques. Most of the risk comes from rushing the SEO checks. Done carefully, the client gets the same site, a faster one, and an editor that comes with WordPress itself.

***Author Bio: ***Fahad Raza is a WordPress developer and SEO consultant based in Sydney. He has built websites since 2005, worked in SEO for more than 18 years, and spent eight and a half years on the IKEA Australia and New Zealand website.

#10343. Scientists discovered the brain doesn't make decisions the way we thought

Scientists at the University of Illinois Urbana Champaign have uncovered evidence that could reshape how researchers think about both the brain and artificial intelligence. Their findings suggest that decision making begins much earlier in the brain than traditional theories propose, offering fresh ideas for designing future AI systems that are more capable and far more energy efficient.

Led by electrical and computer engineering professor Yurii Vlasov at The Grainger College of Engineering, the research was published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Science (PNAS). The study points to an unexpected role for early sensory brain regions in decision making, challenging the long accepted view that decisions emerge only after information moves through a strict hierarchy of brain regions.

The human brain is widely regarded as the most complex structure in the known universe. Scientists still do not fully understand how it works, which is why reverse engineering the brain was identified by the National Academy of Engineering in 2008 as one of the 14 grand challenges for engineering in the 21st century.

For decades, many artificial intelligence systems, including convolutional neural networks, have been inspired by the idea that the brain processes information in a one way sequence. According to this traditional model, sensory information travels upward through increasingly complex brain regions until it reaches the frontal cortex, where decisions are made.

Vlasov and other researchers have increasingly questioned whether that picture is complete.

Instead, they are exploring a model based on natural intelligence, which has been refined through evolution over hundreds of millions of years. In this framework, the brain does not rely only on a step by step flow of information. Decision making also depends on interconnected feedback loops that allow information to move in both directions between brain regions.

Because biological intelligence performs remarkably complex tasks while using far less energy than today's AI systems, understanding this architecture could help guide the development of future artificial intelligence.

"We want to learn from a billion years of evolution," Vlasov said. "How is that biological intelligence organized architecturally? Can we learn from the architectural side of the brain and emulate that to make AI more effective, less power hungry, and more intelligent than it currently is? In the level of decision-making, that's where current AI is lacking."

Early Brain Regions Show Decision Making Activity

To investigate how these processes work, the research team focused on the brain's earliest stages of sensing and perception.

The scientists recorded neural activity in mice as they navigated a virtual reality corridor and made perceptual decisions. They found evidence of decision related activity in the primary somatosensory cortex (S1), one of the brain's earliest sensory processing areas.

Rather than simply passing information forward, S1 appeared to be influenced by higher brain regions through feedback loops. This top down regulation suggests that decision making involves continuous communication across multiple brain areas instead of a simple one direction flow of information.

"The neural code of the brain is still mostly an unknown language," Vlasov said. "But this systems-level understanding can be viewed as a potential impact on how more efficient artificial neural networks can be built -- how the next generation of AI can be thought through. Maybe with these analogies that we learn from real brains, we can improve AI further."

What the Findings Could Mean for Future AI

The researchers emphasize that the study does not provide a blueprint for building better artificial intelligence. Instead, it offers new insights into how the brain organizes decision making that could eventually inspire future AI architectures.

Next, Vlasov and his team plan to investigate the timing of these brain signals in greater detail. They also intend to develop new technologies for measuring neural activity to better understand how feedback loops emerge and coordinate different levels of brain processing.

"By looking at the fast temporal dynamics of neural activity, maybe we can understand better how these feedback loops are engaged in making decisions," Vlasov said. "Maybe that's the approach that potentially uncovers these currently unknown mechanisms -- how these feedback loops are organized dynamically and how they form and shape different levels of processing. Maybe that can be implemented in new architectures for AI."

#10340. Playing GTA 6 this weekend? Here's 16 spoiler-free tips for your first playthrough

It's launch weekend for GTA 6 - in case you hadn't noticed - and since I've played the best part of a hundred hours of this thing, I thought it might be useful to share a few pieces of advice from my time with it.

Many of these are most applicable for the early game, but there are a few that'll be worth bearing in mind throughout. After last night's driving around I would also maybe add in a quick bonus one, come to think of it: watch out for cyclists making last-minute left turns. Or don't, actually. Half of this lot deserve it…

The below list is spoiler-free, so you can relax if you're anxious about going through the story entirely fresh. Though naturally I do explain the way some parts of this game work, taking away some of the sense of discovery. You can take my word for it that there's plenty more to discover beyond this though, so worry not.

If you'd like even more help navigating Leonida, then check out our wonderful guide team's GTA 6 walkthrough.

The number one thing I'd tell people to do in GTA 6 is to create lots of save files and, as you progress and start needing to overwrite them, to try to keep a roughly even spread of files through each chapter. There are various reasons for this - for one, while the game autosaves, it doesn't seem to do that successfully if you suddenly lose power to the console or witness a rare game crash, so it'll preserve your progress. More than that: GTA's story and missions are surprisingly, perhaps mysteriously reactive. Quite a lot can differ, and so being able to go back and make different choices, or play the game differently, will be something 'future you' likely appreciates.

In the very early game you won't have access to a bank account, but once you do: you should put every bit of cash you have in there as soon as you can. Cash is lost on death or arrest - which can happen quite often in GTA 6, funnily enough - and there's no real benefit to carrying it around. Just about everything, besides in-game strippers, can be paid for via your BuckMe account directly. And there's a relatively low $20,000 limit you really don't want to hit in the middle of raiding a gang hideout, either.

GTA 6 has a luxurious range of customisation settings, from hiding notifications about your relationship to reinstating the old 'tap to sprint' control scheme. The accessibility settings - while crucially I'm not an expert - seem considerable. And there are somewhat disguised difficult settings here around enemy damage taken and encounters with the police.

Fairly early in the game you'll gain access to the Scooter Bros. App, which lets you repair or summon your owned vehicles at will. Crucially, there's also an option to pay a one-off fee to unlock three free uses of the app per day. At $12,000, in the early game this is a lot of dosh, but once you rack up that kind of money after advancing through the game a little, it's well worth the initial cost. The sooner you unlock it, the more value it provides over time on a cost-per-use basis. And trust me when I say: as the game's intensity ramps up, you will probably find yourself needing to repair and recover your vehicles quite often. (Also, in Chapter 1, before you get access to the app, you can access the same service by going to your phone's contacts and calling Joey - handy!)

Rockstar has somewhat disincentivised it by adding a cost and putting it in your phone's apps rather than the main map screen, but you can fast travel around Leonida if you ever want or need to. This is done via the RideMe Uber-like app. It's not cheap - you'll need to pay both the fee for the journey and an additional $100 to skip that journey and instantly arrive at your destination, but in certain scenarios it might prove useful. To skip the journey, hold L2/LT once in the cab, and then hold down Triangle/Y when the option is shown. However…

While it's possible to journey-skip your way around this world, having tested that first hand I'd advise against it. It might be obvious, but GTA 6 is genuinely designed around you manually travelling around, typically in the car. If you skip all your commutes between missions or locations, you'll miss out on the game's dozens and dozens of emergent events, which lead to anything from one-off jokes to entire mission chains. The car is also, in a way, kind of the heart of the entire game. Relish the intentional slowness!

Again, avoiding spoilers here, but in the mid game the 'true' loop of GTA 6 gameplay will properly reveal itself, in all the many methods of earning money and the increased emphasis on doing so. You can of course play the game however you like, but having reached the end and looked back from that point, I found that if there was a particular moment to set aside as the time for aimlessly exploring the world, it was from around Chapter 3 onwards. You'll have enough tools to be able to see it at more or less its fullest then, but also won't have missed anything essential by waiting until that point to take your foot off the pedal either.

A handy early-game tip here that even I missed when I was playing, but have since discovered: two islands in the small cluster of them to the south-west of Jason's early game home each house a really useful weapon, in a silenced pistol and a handy shotgun. You'll own these permanently once found, and so they can be incredibly helpful for navigating missions with maximum or minimal violence. Look for shipwrecks on those islands to find them. The pistol is hidden under a little hatch on the deck of a shipwreck on the southernmost point of the south-easternmost island. The shotgun is next to a small wooden wrecked boat around the middle of the northernmost island.

A mechanic I slightly underused at first was the ability to 'save' a given outfit to your car. You can do this either from your car's trunk or from the wardrobe, and it's hugely useful as you start to get into more elaborate scrapes with the police (and also if you just like to role-play a bit and don the right outfit for the right occasion).

There are lots of reasons for this, from the moments of intimacy it affords you with your partner, to the extra buffs you can get from resting. Sleep at home, for instance, and you can then immediately pet your snake (ahem), down a coffee or drink from the fridge, grab an apple and take a shower for a range of buffs across health, stamina, and focus. Each of these will last quite some time, so it's worth the few minutes of time to do them. Eating and drinking regularly also helps you maximise gains in the gym.

Rockstar seems to enjoy the concept of a game within a game, and that's exemplified well by the in-game phone. You can find missions via scrolling Snapmatic, it's in-game social media, or from texting various contacts you pick up as the game progresses. It's worth checking it every now and then just to see if anything interesting - or just funny or absurd - might pop up.

Car trunks, both those belonging to the public and the police, are often well worth a look. Even if you're quickly nabbing a car for a short-term dash, take a moment to check the boot for anything worthwhile. We've found everything from sellable narcotics to very useful weapons in there. In cop cars, that goes up several notches, too.

A small thing, but in-mission checkpoints are relatively generous in GTA 6. If you really wanted to complete a mission a certain way - undetected or non-violent, say - then don't be afraid to quickly re-load rather than feeling you need to manually load up an earlier save, or give up on your goal entirely. It's also helped me out with a few minor progress-jamming bugs along the way too.

This might seem obvious, but it's worth emphasising for early-game players: it's very, very rare that you actually need to kill anybody in GTA 6. Enemies are fully incapacitated when you see a yellow hit marker over your crosshairs, even if that just comes from blasting away at their toes. If you make a habit of navigating combat this way then that also makes it much easier to recover your 'Professional' criminal status if you ever do decide to go full rampage. Though you can, of course, ultimately play this game however you like. Just be aware there may be consequences, known and unknown, as you go. Also: don't forget to click the right analog stick to aim down sights - it's an easy thing to forget when playing a third-person shooter like this, and not always the best way to operate, but incredibly helpful in select circumstances.

Throughout the game you'll have a 'family savings' goal to hit. As you progress you'll find more ways to earn money much faster, and so it's easy to make up for lost time here if, later on, you decide that actually you do want to think about the future after all. But that grind will be a fair bit less painful if you chip away at the target as you go. As long as you save yourself some fun money - a few hundred in the early game, few thousand in the mid game, and a few tens of thousands late on - then you'll have enough to do key things like buying new garages to register vehicles, or paying to register them themselves.

Throughout your time with GTA 6 you'll encounter moments when you need to make a choice. Interestingly, I noticed at least a few occasions where a scenario changed when I just waited, doing nothing at all. Sometimes that might mean a choice is made for you - so waiting is a risk - but on other occasions new options become available. Sometimes they might mean a genuinely different consequence, others they might just lead to characters reacting in a certain kind of way. But it's worth experimenting - your first options aren't always your only ones.

#10337. I completed GTA 6's indie game darling pastiche, Tenebrae Lux, and all I got was this lousy sense of accomplishment

"We are but Promethean wanderers on the fringes of oblivion, clinging to a semblance of light amidst the vast abyss of our own ignorance. Voyaging uncharted waters may appear foolish to some, yet folly and heroism can often appear the same to the undiscerning eye," so says the voice of Johannes Zuch - creator, writer, director, composer, and 'perceptual architect' behind Leonida's latest favourite indie darling art game, Tenebrae Lux. It's pretentious, it's deeply up its own arse, and it's awkward and off-putting to play. A must-review for Eurogamer.

Developed, seemingly single-handedly, by an eccentric developer called Johannes Zuch - auteur, pseud, charlatan - you first get introduced to this curious little experiment in one of GTA 6's earliest missions, where protagonist Jason is forced to play it during a 'lad's night in' with buddy Cal. Jason is quick to dismiss Tenebrae Lux in company, but once Cal slinks off home - hungover and dreary - I slide the disc back into my JoyStation console and sink my teeth back into it. Jason loves this stuff, really. He only keeps Time Jackers: Rewind installed so his mates don't judge him.

The first thing I notice about Tenebrae Lux is the name. It's Latin for 'darkness and light', or something similar. Is this riffing on Clair Obscur, which is French for 'light dark'? No, it's too cerebral for that - too plodding and navel-gazey. Sandfall Interactive wouldn't be this pretentious. Maybe it's a pastiche of Dear Esther, then, drawing on the tenets and schema of the 'walking simulator' genre and using that washed-out film noir aesthetic. But then, it's too wordy for that, with too many interactive and puzzle-adjacent elements. Ah, it must be mocking The Witness, instead - there's the telltale lighthouse, the 'I'm definitely not telling you where to go and what to do' internal narration, and of course the fingerprints of Johannes Zuch are all over it. Johannes Zuch, Jonathan Blow - see how they braided them together? (Sorry).

Whilst this has been created by Rockstar as a pastiche - as much loving send-up as it is withering take down - and designed to make a quick joke in the early 'Feng Shui' mission, the game is playable from start to finish if you so desire. You boot it up by inserting a physical disc, too, which is funny given the context. And it's good! Well, not good good, but it's a proper brainteaser, and ribs 2016's The Witness with such knowledge and (I think?) respect that it's hard not to be charmed by Rockstar's game-within-a-game. There are collectibles to be found that riff on Mark Z. Danielewski's House of Leaves, too, a knowing nod to the most try-hard of all try-hard literature.

Within seconds of the title screen, too, you're presented with a game-within-a-game-within-a-game. You must clear four boards filled with puzzle pieces as the protagonist mutters something mysterious and weird in his posh voice. Do so, and you unlock the door to the next location. Head up to a bunker, and you'll see a room filled with various clues - maybe it's a flashing lamp flickering in morse code, maybe it's a malfunctioning clock presenting a maths puzzle, maybe it's a pricetag on a record that changes on every visit, maybe it's a photograph with anomalous elements, maybe it's a "Developed Using Zuchworks Engine" easter egg hidden in the environment. You need to keep your wits about you, because one of these clues changes every time you enter - and the clue corresponds to a date that changes on a calendar on the wall.

You can look up a guide if you need to, or you can spend far too long figuring out how all this relates to the telephone you can find in the room on your own, like muggins here, before opening up the path to the next puzzle. Look at the image below to see the level of record-keeping and brainteasing this bizarre little game prompted from me. I will say, the sense of achievement you get from playing around with this stuff is pretty remarkable, given - let's not forget I'm actually playing Grand Theft Auto 6 whilst I'm wandering around in the black and white murk trying to complete a puzzle game for no actual reward.

The bunker room is, by far, the hardest part of Tenebrae Lux. From here, things ease up: you need to figure out the right sequence of glyphs on a bridge, and then put some distance between yourself and a curious and rather creepy suited man that's seemingly figuring things out ahead of you in a location inspired by, I think, The Backrooms (or Portal, or Superliminal, or maybe something else entirely. Who knows what Zuch was thinking?)

"With the last enigma finally mastered," the narrator drones in his bumbling monotone, "I step forward into the void, the shadows swallow, consuming all, and then finally the sweet embrace of darkness of which there is no end." 'You have just experienced a Johannes Zuch experience', Tenebrae Lux tells me, before cutting to the best joke of the whole thing: the credits roll much akin to something Hideo Kojima would produce.

So, what do you get out of all of this? Well - just like real puzzle games in the real world - nothing, really. If you've not completed one of the other three fully playable games in GTA 6, you will get a trophy/achievement. But given the main game is all about Jason and Lucia's desperate scramble to escape the poverty trap, to try and break free of the cycle of debt, violence, and consequence that keeps them clinging to Leonida's seedy underbelly, there's no monetary reward. There's no 'progress' in the sense of the protagonist's shared story.

Even in terms of your own cold, hard, mathematical 'completion' you only need to boot each of the four games up once in order to work towards GTA 6's 100% completion. So what's the point of all this? Why did I spend the better part of 90 minutes trying to figure out how to find a sliver of light in the dark in Tenebrae Lux? The game is a wonderful pastiche in that, essentially, it's not really saying anything. You can probably project some vague meaning onto it if you wish - I'm pretty certain the protagonist literally 'finds himself' at the end - but glib little readings like that are ten-a-penny in this genre.

I think the most impressive thing about Tenebrae Lux is that it exists. You're teased with it in an early mission - Rockstar may as well say 'look, we put a game in a game, lol' - but it's more than that. This is what happens when Rockstar's 4700-plus developers are given the room to… develop. Tenebrae Lux could very easily have been a non-interactive experience, a quick, cheap joke shown over-the-shoulder taking a drive-by pop shot at Johnathan Blow, Hideo Kojima, Dan Pinchbeck, or any and all of the above. Or maybe it could be a 'vertical slice', an incomplete demo, a teaser. But it's not, because nothing about GTA 6 is quick or cheap.

GTA 6, in every single conceivable way, is a premium experience - part-sandbox, part-simulation, part-otherworld. To create not just one, but four fully playable and completable games within that framework is showboating, sure, but to make that game actually good and - perhaps controversially - even better than some of the games it's pastiching… Well, it's just rubbing salt in the wound, really.

A code for the game was provided by Cal Hampton.

#10336. Alan Turing's biggest AI assumption may have been wrong

Alan Turing's famous ideas about artificial intelligence may have sent AI research down the wrong path for the past 75 years, according to prominent computer scientist Peter J. Denning.

In his new book, Turing's Mistake: Escaping the Yoke of Unintelligent Machines, Denning argues that two foundational assumptions made by Turing in 1950 continue to shape AI research today. The first is that intelligence can exist independently of a physical body and therefore be recreated in computer software. The second is that a machine can demonstrate intelligence by successfully imitating a human in conversation, an idea that later became known as the Turing test.

"These two claims have shaped much of AI research and development," Denning writes. "My premise is that our acquiescence to these claims has led to the AI mess in which we find ourselves today."

Denning argues that pursuing artificial general intelligence (AGI), or machines with human level intelligence, is unlikely to succeed. Instead, he warns, the technologies society is building could introduce significant new risks.

At the heart of Denning's argument is the idea of tacit knowledge, the vast amount of human understanding that cannot easily be put into words or represented in a form that computers can process.

He says machine learning cannot capture five major categories of tacit knowledge: common sense, everyday interactions with people and the environment, emotions and perception, practical performance skills, and the social and historical knowledge embedded in culture.

Researchers have long attempted to organize common sense into databases. One of the best known efforts was Douglas Lenat's Cyc project, which began in the 1980s with the goal of creating an extensive collection of common sense facts. After four decades of work, the project contained roughly 25 million entries.

"Yet even this treasury could not add up to a background of common sense sufficient to make expert systems smart enough to be experts," Denning notes. "Cyc validated that much of the knowledge that makes people experts cannot be articulated as propositions."

Denning believes practical skills present an even greater challenge.

"Our performance skills in thousands of domains cannot be communicated to machines," he explains. "Whereas descriptions of skillful outcomes ('know what') can often be represented as bits and stored in a machine, we do not know how to encode the embodied knowledge for skillful performance ('know how')."

He points to accomplished musicians as an example.

"A virtuoso violinist can play beautiful music yet cannot describe to an acolyte how to produce it.

"Even if a robot could observe and imitate skilled humans, having no biological body, a robot cannot grasp how the musician feels when playing beautiful music or how an audience feels when hearing it."

Denning also includes intuition, gut feelings, imagination, and spontaneous creativity among the forms of tacit knowledge that remain beyond the reach of machines.

Denning argues that all of these limitations stem from what he calls the "representation problem."

Computers can only perform calculations using data and instructions that have been encoded into physical forms they can recognize and process. Tacit knowledge, however, does not naturally fit into that framework.

"Behind every word is a deep well of tacit knowledge that gives it meaning," Denning says. "Words are but symbolic representations of meanings, not the meanings themselves. Commonly used Large Language Models, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini only manipulate words, they cannot know or understand the meaning of what they are saying."

According to Denning, this creates a fundamental divide. Because scientists still cannot fully explain how tacit knowledge works in humans, they also cannot translate it into a form machines can use.

"How we host tacit knowledge is largely a mystery," Denning admits. "All we know is that it is embodied. We have no idea what we might observe and measure in our bodies to reveal it."

Denning also argues that intelligence depends heavily on context, the surrounding circumstances that give words, actions, and decisions their meaning.

Context allows people to recognize sarcasm, humor, sincerity, and emotion. It helps determine when to be diplomatic, when to joke, and how to interpret countless social cues.

"When you inquire into where an assumption of the current context came from, you discover it rests on previous conversations from previous contexts. Each of those in turn rests on further previous conversations and their contexts. This pattern is endless and fractal," Denning explains.

Culture presents another major obstacle for AI.

Denning describes culture as encompassing values, norms, judgments, history, communities, moods, and even relationships involving power and care.

"Human conversations are imbued with background assumptions that give meaning and relevance to the words being used," Denning explains.

"Scaling up LLMs with ever larger neural networks will not enable them to acquire the embodied human knowledge we call culture. LLMs will not attain the objective of the Turing test: to demonstrate machine thought indistinguishable from human thought."

AI Safety and the Limits of Human Understanding

Denning concludes that humans and AI systems may ultimately develop different forms of tacit knowledge that neither can fully understand.

"Machines cannot read our tacit knowledge and we cannot read theirs," he writes. "We are aliens across an uncrossable divide."

He argues this gap raises serious concerns about AI safety. If machines cannot interpret the unspoken context behind human intentions, reliably aligning advanced AI systems with human goals may prove impossible.

"Through AI automation, agentic networks of machines are likely to develop their own machine intelligence that does not reach the level of human general intelligence but is still quite capable of creating severe problems for humans. This threat is a greater than a take-over by superintelligent machines," he explains.

"Machine intelligence has different concerns from us and does not appear to care about us. Its ways of thinking and problem-solving look alien to us. We do not yet know how to live safely with these machines.

"Pulling back from an AI automation singularity will demand much from us. We start by accepting that the familiar culture is fading away as intelligent machines appear in our society and we do not know what is coming. We decline to think like machines or be subservient to machines. We refuse to submit to a yoke imposed by low-intelligence machines. Most importantly, we reassert our humanity, declare once again what makes us different from machines, and celebrate those differences."

Materials provided by Taylor & Francis Group. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10335. At $600, the Pixel 10 is this year’s no-brainer Black Friday smartphone deal

Phones have gotten a lot more expensive over the last year or so, and it’s a trend we’re expecting to get worse before it can get better. If you’re in the market for an upgrade, this year’s Black Friday might be one of the final truly good times to buy a new device, and for just $600, last year’s Pixel 10 should be high on your list.

While buying year-old hardware typically comes with some pretty deep sacrifices between generations, that’s not particularly true with the Pixel 10 this year. From a hardware perspective, nearly everything is either identical or close enough to not particularly matter. Its design and display are all but unchanged, Qi2-ready magnets come on both models, and both devices are built with the same level of battery longevity in mind. And much to the chagrin of many a Pixel die-hard, Tensor G5 and Tensor G6 are practically interchangeable.

So what are you giving up that matters? When the Pixel 11 arrived, software features made up the bulk of this list, but with last week’s Pixel Drop, a lot of the gaps between these two generations have been closed. Gemini Intelligence with Rambler, app automation, and more are in the process of rolling out to existing Pixel 10 users, and new features like Create My Widget arrived on the Pixel 10 and 11 at the exact same time. From a software perspective — Google’s bread and butter, in my eyes — the only big sacrifice comes from the year of software support that’s already complete, leaving you with just six instead of seven.

Realistically, the camera is the one place you’re likely to feel a difference. The Pixel 10 was the first non-Pro device in Google’s Tensor era to ship with a telephoto lens, but it came with some big sacrifices. The main sensor is effectively an A-series lens, and taken together, the entire package might leave something to be desired. It’s far from a bad camera though — I used it as my main shooter through most of its lifecycle — and while the Pixel 11 did get some upgrades here, I think real shutterbugs would be better off looking at Google’s Pro lineup anyway. You’ll also lose out on things like HiLight, though really, are you missing that much?

What makes this deal so good is really its place in the market, not as a direct comparison to the newer Pixel 11. For $600, Google’s competition is going to have a hard time competing with the value the Pixel 10 delivers. Hell, even Google might find it difficult to compete in the coming months; at full price, $600 is what the Pixel 10a goes for now, a decidedly less-impressive device compared to this model. No, this is a flagship smartphone through and through, and for $600, you’re effectively guaranteeing a reliable, powerful smartphone experience from now until 2032 — hopefully enough time for this whole RAM crisis to finally simmer down a bit.

#10333. It took me less than an hour to find my first incredibly minor Rockstar easter egg in GTA 6 - but it has some big implications for Leonida

Are you wondering how connected the worlds of GTA 5 and GTA 6 are? Well, I've got some news for you. Keep on reading below if you'd like some very minor spoilers for the early game of GTA 6, spoilers for GTA 5, as well as some information about how the new game links to GTA 5 and other Rockstar games.

Right, if you're reading from this point onwards, you're clearly here for the tea. In the first hour or so of GTA 6, when you finally get control of Jason and head to your first property (the green stilted house) in the Leonida Keys, you will be able to explore a little. On my way to do a workout - you need to keep Jason a peak physical instrument for his work's sake, right? Right? - I happened upon a fitness magazine resting on a table on the decking out front.

Called 'Body Copy' - a joke I appreciate as a former magazine editor, naturally - this publication features a few different articles. There's Morning Glory, where Nolan Crockett jacks you with his early workout; Skindecent Exposure, a photo spread about why beaches are 'crazy' places to work out; Shrediquette, a piece dedicated to proper in-gym decorum; and Twilight Tantra, an interview feature and yoga masterclass with 'gerontophile' Fabien LaRouche.

Hang on, Fabien LaRouche… isn't that the French wellness guru and shyster that was a "close friend" to Amanda De Santa in Grand Theft Auto 5? Yes, yes it is. In fact, Fabien played quite a large role in that game, acting as the antagonistic force that eventually fractured Michael and Amanda's relationship. After conducting an affair under the guise of 'yoga lessons', Amanda left our protagonist, and moved in with Fabien, taking Michael's kids - Jimmy and Tracy - with her. In a totally healthy and normal way, you could follow their new life via updates posted to GTA's Facebook surrogate, LifeInvader. It's clear the kids never liked the pretentious, annoying man - but for Amanda, the penny is a little slower to drop. Eventually, Amanda and Michael reconcile their differences - with the latter whalloping Fabien in the process. The married couple pledge to resolve their differences, and Fabien is never seen again.

Until GTA 6, at least. Here, in what we assume is supposed to be 2025 or 2026, it's been about 13 years since we last saw the character (it is widely agreed that GTA 5 is set in 2013 - the game's original launch year). And it seems that the events surrounding Michael and his family really did a number on Fabien. Which - of course - he blamed on the universe, rather than taking any personal responsibility. Naturally.

"Ever since the karmic decay of Los Santos was made perfectly clear to him in the early 2010s, yoga instructor Fabien LaRouche has been on an epic pilgrimage of enlightenment through the remotest ashrams and finest 5-star resorts and plastic surgery retreats of The East," reads the Body Copy article. "Having completed his chakric education and returned to the United States, we meet with him on the final week of his six-month residency at Dwindle Wood Retirement Community."

Here, the article goes on to explore Fabien's penchant for older women - he seems to like their nature, their desire to learn about self-improvement and wellness, and (perhaps most importantly) their bank accounts. "Being over the hill doesn't necessarily mean you have nothing left to live for," he opines in the article. Thanks for that, Fabien.

It's interesting to see - very early in the game and quite plainly telegraphed - that Rockstar is willing to reintroduce us to people from previous games. This isn't a megaton addition by any means - Fabien was never a 'main character' - but I love that a nod to him, in a feature tucked away at the back of a magazine, sets the scene for more cameos, perhaps, later in the game. It shows us, nice and early, that GTA 5 and GTA 6 are indeed connected. By inference, then, we know that GTA 4 is included in that same picture; there were recurring characters in GTA 5 that appeared in GTA 4, after all - Patrick McReary, Johnny Klebitz, Rocco Pelosi and more come to mind.

It may seem like a small thing, but it's just another example of Rockstar using its expansive toolset, ridiculous budget, and well-established legacy to inject a sense of scale into the world of Grand Theft Auto 6. There are other nods to the universe out there, too. I won't spoil them here, but I've been a little bit dewy-eyed to hear rumours of some of the other nods to Rockstar titles hidden in the world of Leonida: it makes all the experiences I've had in past games, the emotional response I've had to previous Rockstar worlds, feel in some way valid and meaningful here, too. I'm looking forward to seeing what other little secrets await me across the keys and into the glowing neon promise of Vice City proper.

#10332. What we've been playing - "It's slow, it's awkward, it's weird, and it's hard"

A few of the things that have us hooked this week.

Did anything notable happen this week? Not that I can remember. The weather was quite rainy - will that do? I'm just being silly, of course. We've had - and I suppose are still having - an historic week in video games, as Grand Theft Auto 6 arrives. It's dominated everything and I fear it's going to dominate this article too. But a reminder: next week is our "Not-GTA Week", so we'll be making a concerted effort to talk about games, probably smaller games, that aren't Godzilla blockbusters.

As you know, this is our regular feature where we say a bit about the games we've been playing this week. This week, rather a lot of us have been playing GTA 6, as you can imagine, and discovering various things about it. But not all of us. Connor, ever the contrarian, has been continuing his race to level 60 in World of Warcraft: Forever, and he's agonisingly close to getting there.

But enough about us, what about you? What have you been playing this week? Do tell all! And don't forget we have an entire archive of previous What We've Been Playings for your leisurely perusal, just in case you forgot what you were playing a year or a month or a week ago.

It probably comes as no surprise that I'm - much like the rest of the world - playing GTA 6 right now. While I found Chapter 1 to be quite a slow start, and where I felt somewhat restricted, I've now started Chapter 2 and found myself enjoying stealing cars, jamming along to the radio, and simply exploring Leonida - and all the strange happenings that come with it. There's so much to see and do!

I'm looking forward to deviating from the main missions for a while to do a spot of bird-watching (I like birds a lot, alright) and seeing what other side activities Leonida has to offer outside of the criminal lifestyle at the core of things. I'm also trying to be the best partner possible to both Jason and Lucia, but I'm itching to cause a bit of trouble soon... Hurting NPCs comes with so much guilt this time around though!

It's slow, it's awkward, it's weird, and it's hard. It's a perfect Eurogamer game, right? Right? GTA 6's in-game lampoon of Jonathan Blow, Hideo Kojima, Dan Pinchbeck and - weirdly - Mark Z. Danielewski is a wonderful bit of top-shelf pastiche. It goes to show just how much fun Rockstar had making GTA 6, and the freedom its dev team had to install as much depth and satire in just about every nook and cranny conceivable. Don't sleep on Tenebrae Lux, it's genuinely satisfying to complete.

I'm not, historically, the biggest GTA fan - although I've absolutely got a soft spot for Vice City's sublime mood - so I wasn't quite as excited to play GTA 6 as some. But it took, oh I dunno, about 30 seconds before I was sold. This thing has style. And everything else a billion dollars and some incredible development talent gets you. And it's those because-we-can details that have, in my first few hours, left the biggest impression. I spent a good five minutes just marveling at Jason dance - specifically the way his little stationary wiggle (perfectly timed to the radio beat!) shifts seamlessly into a wiggle-strut when you hit the forward button.

I love the way the setting sun seems to shine just right through the clouds when the moment calls, and those perfect needle drops. And careening through the night - amid the driving rain and smear of taillights, Kylie classic Spinning Around booming on the radio and Jason rocking a recently acquired, slightly improbable hat - this extravagant, ridiculous thing had me completely transfixed. I'm genuinely, unexpectedly excited to see where it takes me next.

Assuming there's lots of Grand Theft Auto 6 in this article, I'll save you from my own early impressions of this week's blockbuster release. Instead, you get more tales from an MMO. It is what it is!

I'm level 58 right now, pushing my way into the endgame dungeons. I've almost maxed all my professions, and am gradually getting gear that should serve me well when the raids are added next month.

But forget all that. I got a salt shaker! As a leatherworker, you can buy a salt shaker from engineers for a little bit of gold on the auction house. These are more important than you'd assume. With them you can make one refined deeprock salt every three days - a high-end crafting material. Rather than hoard these for fancy gear, I just sold 'em back to the auction house. They're current going for 50 gold a pop on my server, which is fantastic passive income.

This is important because I'm currently saving for an epic mount: a process that hit a major roadbump after I unlocked my secondary class specialisation for 50 gold, and then blew way more than that on unlocking all the available skills (that I likely won't use) from my druid trainer (for no good reason). I'm currently sitting on 232 gold as of writing. There's a long way to go to 1000, but hey, that's the game.

I can't imagine anyone changing the radio station when Drive by The Cars begins during that first moment of proper uninterrupted freedom. The buttons to do that might as well not even be there. If you did, we're completely different people.

I'm not very far in but my major impressions of GTA 6 so far are: the performances and their presentation are wonderful, the game controls a bit sludgily and feels like it's not quite in focus on PS5, and I really like DIY.

Let's take that middle one, that criticism: I'm sure this will lift as I get used to the game and how it moves, and how the characters work. It's also just a fact of life, so to speak, that it's going to struggle a bit on PS5 rather than PS5 Pro. And I'm nitpicking; on the whole, this thing is staggeringly technically impressive.

The latter point, DIY: it's absurd how much detail Rockstar has put into you doing up your shack. I especially like how it's not boring. A deeper thought related to this, and to the rest of the game, is the fantasy of self-improvement GTA 6 delivers. In GTA 6, as in all GTA games I think, you can drastically alter your life's fortunes in mere moments. I set about doing up my shack in a way I could never do in real life given a week or a month, but here, I did it in moments. That appeals to me greatly.

Honourable mention to Star Wars: Galactic Racer which I finally played this week. Love the speed, love Biddy Blas, and also really gel with the Roguelike approach, whereby you take the game in 'runs' to see how far you can progress each time. Cracking game.

#10330. New programmable photonic chip can control how fast light moves

Researchers at Seoul National University and the University of Seoul have developed a programmable photonic integrated circuit that can slow light whenever needed.

The team was led by Professors Namkyoo Park and Sunkyu Yu of the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Seoul National University, working with Professor Xianji Piao of the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of Seoul.

Slowing Light Could Help Solve a Computing Bottleneck

The rapid growth of generative AI and large scale AI models has sharply increased the amount of computing power required by data centers and servers. Conventional electronic semiconductors are struggling to keep pace because they consume large amounts of energy and face limits in how quickly they can transmit data.

These challenges have intensified interest in optical computing, which uses light rather than electrical signals to process information. Optical systems could potentially move data at extremely high speeds while using less power.

However, light also presents a major challenge. Because it naturally moves at a fixed speed, it is difficult to delay optical signals or temporarily hold them in place. Those capabilities are essential for creating buffers and memory functions in optical computers.

To address this problem, the researchers designed a programmable photonic circuit that can control both the speed and shape of optical signals. Their approach provides more flexibility over "slow light" than previously proposed methods.

The study was published in the renowned international journal Advanced Science.

Why Optical Signals Sometimes Need To Wait

Photonic integrated circuits are emerging as a promising technology for processing information quickly and efficiently with light. In data centers, optical communication networks, and future computing systems, moving signals rapidly is only part of the challenge.

Systems must also ensure that different signals arrive at the correct time. In some cases, a light signal must be delayed so it can remain synchronized with other information moving through the system.

One method for creating these delays relies on coupled-resonator-induced transparency (CRIT), which uses interference among several optical resonators.

CRIT allows light within a selected frequency range to pass through a device while also reducing the speed at which the optical signal travels.

Traditional CRIT devices usually have operating characteristics that become permanent once they are manufactured. This makes it difficult to change how they function after fabrication.

For example, engineers who want to create a longer signal delay or work with a different frequency range often need to design and manufacture an entirely new photonic device.

That lack of adaptability increases the complexity of optical communication hardware and data center infrastructure. It can also raise costs and extend development schedules whenever new capabilities are needed.

The problem is especially important for AI servers and next-generation data centers, where enormous amounts of information must be processed in real time. Fixed optical components have therefore remained a major obstacle to more practical optical computing systems.

A Programmable Design for Controlling Light

The research team developed a different strategy by treating two optical states in CRIT systems, known as the bright mode and dark mode, as one unified degree of freedom. The researchers also added two controllable loop couplers.

Together, these changes created a new design principle for programmable photonic integrated circuits. Resonator arrangements that were previously locked into one configuration after fabrication could instead be adjusted for different purposes.

Using the new CRIT structure, the researchers showed that the movement of light could be delayed and controlled as needed. They also demonstrated that interference between the bright and dark modes could be handled as a single integrated design parameter.

This approach greatly expanded the flexibility of photonic resonator circuits that had previously been limited by fixed designs.

Controlling Delay, Bandwidth, and Signal Shape

The researchers theoretically demonstrated that the two loop couplers could be used to adjust the bandwidth and shape of the passband. They could also control how long signals were delayed and how efficiently those signals traveled through the circuit.

This means that both the speed and transmission behavior of optical signals could be reconfigured across entire systems containing multiple resonators, rather than only within a single resonator.

Numerical simulations also showed that the speed of optical pulses could be adjusted dynamically while the circuit was operating.

The results indicated that signal delay times could be changed without reducing processing performance. The system could also convert the frequency of light without requiring additional specialized components.

Simulations Suggest the Chip Could Be Practical

The researchers used three-dimensional electromagnetic simulations to test whether the CRIT device could be built on a silicon nitride (Si3N4) photonic integrated circuit platform.

They also evaluated a range of real-world issues that could affect the device during manufacturing and operation. These included material losses, differences in resonator quality, backscattering, coupling fluctuations, phase errors in the loop couplers, and thermal crosstalk.

The simulations indicated that the proposed structure could continue to operate reliably under realistic conditions.

One Chip Could Perform Several Optical Functions

The study introduces a programmable photonic platform that can control both the timing and frequency properties of light signals in real time.

The design could overcome the limitations of conventional optical delay devices, which typically perform only fixed functions. It also suggests that several important capabilities could eventually be combined within one photonic circuit.

These functions include signal synchronization, adjustable delay lines, optical buffers, and frequency conversion.

The same design principles may also be useful beyond CRIT systems. The researchers believe the approach could be applied to a broad range of photonic circuits based on resonators, potentially providing a foundation for more adaptable optical signal processing technologies.

Potential Benefits for AI and Data Centers

If the technology is commercialized, a single programmable optical chip could perform several tasks, including controlling signal speed and switching between different functions.

In that sense, the chip could operate in a way similar to a software-defined system, with its behavior adjusted according to changing needs.

This flexibility could help data centers and AI servers process information more efficiently while reducing energy consumption.

Combining several signal processing functions on one chip could also make optical communication equipment and sensor systems smaller and less expensive.

Over the longer term, the technology could support industries that depend on extremely fast information processing, including autonomous driving, next-generation communications, and quantum technologies.

Researchers Plan Larger Programmable Photonic Systems

Professor Namkyoo Park, co-corresponding author of the study from Seoul National University, stated, "This research is significant in that it proposes a new design principle that allows the flow of light within photonic integrated circuits to be reconfigured as needed, greatly enhancing design flexibility. We plan to expand this technology toward large-scale programmable photonic integrated circuits based on silicon photonics and photonic AI technologies."

Co-first authors Dr. Seungkyun Park and Ph.D. student Beomjoon Chae, who led the theoretical framework and numerical analysis, added, "Through this study, we realized that reinterpreting conventional photonic resonator physics from a different perspective can serve as a starting point for discovering new functionalities in photonic integrated circuits. We plan to further develop this research toward practical device implementation and experimental validation."

Dr. Seungkyun Park is affiliated with the InnoCORE PICORE Center at KAIST and is currently conducting research on photonic AI and quantum optics at the Photonic Systems Laboratory, Seoul National University.

Ph.D. student Beomjoon Chae is conducting research on programmable photonic integrated circuits at the Intelligent Wave Systems Laboratory, SNU.

The research received support from the Ministry of Science and ICT through the Innovative Research Center (IRC) program, the Basic Research Laboratory (BRL) program, and the Young Researcher Program.

Dr. Seungkyun Park also participated in the study with support from the InnoCORE program (PICORE Center).

Materials provided by Seoul National University College of Engineering. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10329. Automating Contract Signing in Node.js: Webhooks, Verification, and Storing Signed PDFs

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sending a document for signature is the easy part of an e-signature integration. One POST request and the signer gets an email. The work that actually breaks in production happens afterwards: knowing when the document was signed, trusting the notification that told you so, handling the same notification twice, and getting the final PDF into storage before the download link expires.

This tutorial builds that whole loop in Node.js with Express. An event in your app (a deal is approved, a client is onboarded, a task moves to "ready to sign") sends a contract from a template. When the signer finishes, a webhook arrives, your server verifies it, and the signed PDF plus its audit trail get saved without anyone touching them.

The code uses Firma.dev, the e-signature API I work on, because I needed a real API to make the examples runnable. The patterns are not specific to it, though. Signature verification, idempotent handlers, short-lived download URLs, and reconciliation jobs show up in almost every webhook-driven integration, and the same structure applies whether you're receiving events from a payment processor, a CI system, or another signing provider.

There's a fifth part that tutorials usually skip: a reconciliation job that catches anything the webhooks missed. We'll build that too, because webhooks are a notification mechanism, not a delivery guarantee.

Before sending anything, wrap the HTTP calls in one place. This is where authentication lives, and it's also where you handle 429 Too Many Requests once instead of in every caller. Most APIs, this one included, return a Retry-After header on a 429, so the client should honour it rather than guessing a backoff.

The 503 branch matters later. When a document has just been completed, the final PDF and its completion certificate take a moment to generate, and the download endpoint says so with a 503 and a Retry-After instead of handing you a half-built file.

The trigger depends on your product. It might be a route handler, a queue consumer, or a CRM automation calling into your service. What matters is that the function doing the sending is small and takes plain data:

Two design choices are worth calling out.

Use a single create-and-send call when you can. Many signing APIs split this into "create a draft" and "send the draft." That's useful when a human needs to review the document first, but for automation it creates a window where your process can crash between the two calls and leave an orphaned draft. A combined endpoint makes the operation atomic from your side.

Store the provider's ID on your own record immediately. Webhook payloads reference the signing request, not your deal or customer. Without that mapping you'll end up searching by email address, which falls apart as soon as one client signs two documents.

Here's the first place integrations quietly go wrong. Webhook signatures are computed over the exact bytes the sender transmitted. If Express parses the body as JSON first, you lose those bytes, and re-serialising the object won't reproduce them (key order, whitespace, and number formatting can all change). Signature checks then fail intermittently, which is the worst kind of failure.

The fix is to use express.raw() on the webhook route only, so the handler receives a Buffer:

Most webhook providers sign payloads with HMAC-SHA256 using a shared secret. The details vary, so read your provider's docs for the exact header format, but the scheme here is common: the header looks like t=1731456000,v1=5f2b..., and the signed string is the timestamp, a dot, and the raw body. Stripe uses a very similar format, and the Standard Webhooks spec describes the same idea as a vendor-neutral convention.

Each line here defends against something specific.

The OWASP guidance on cryptographic storage covers the other half of this: the secret belongs in an environment variable or secrets manager, never in the repository.

Every serious webhook system delivers at least once, not exactly once. If your endpoint is slow, returns a 5xx, or the network drops the response, the sender retries. Firma.dev, for example, makes up to three attempts per event (immediately, then after at least five minutes, then after at least an hour) and treats anything other than a 2xx as a failure, including redirects. Other providers retry more aggressively. Either way, your handler will eventually see the same event twice.

The defence is to record each event's unique ID and skip ones you've seen. In the server above that's alreadyProcessed and markProcessed. For a demo, a Set works:

In production, use your database and let a unique constraint do the work, so two concurrent deliveries can't both pass the check:

Also notice the order in the route: respond with 200, then do the work. Many providers time out deliveries after a few seconds (five, in this case). Downloading a PDF and uploading it to object storage can easily take longer than that, and a timeout counts as a failure, which triggers a retry, which triggers duplicate work. Acknowledging fast and processing asynchronously avoids that loop.

setImmediate is fine for a tutorial, but it has a real weakness: if the process dies after sending the 200 and before finishing the work, the event is acknowledged and lost. In production, push the event onto a durable queue (BullMQ, SQS, a jobs table) before responding. Step 7 covers the safety net for whatever still slips through.

Now the actual business logic. You'll usually see several event types (sent, viewed, a signer signed, declined, expired, completed). Only one of them means "the document is final":

Three things in here are easy to get wrong.

Don't treat "a signer signed" as "the document is done." With multiple signers, each one triggers its own event, and a per-signer "all complete" flag can be true on more than one of them. Key your storage logic off the single completion event.

Don't persist the download URL. Pre-signed URLs expire (this one carries an expires_at). Saving the link to your database and serving it to users later produces broken links a few minutes or hours later. Download the bytes and store them in storage you control. Swapping the fs.writeFile calls for an S3 PutObject or a Google Drive upload is a drop-in change.

Store the audit trail, not just the PDF. If a signature is ever disputed, the PDF shows what was signed, and the audit trail shows who signed it, when, and from where (timestamps, IP addresses, the sequence of views and signatures). That evidence is what makes an electronic signature defensible, which brings us to the legal side.

Retries are finite. Endpoints go down during deploys. Some providers auto-disable a webhook after enough consecutive failures, and events aren't guaranteed to arrive in order. Any one of these can leave a completed document sitting unsaved.

A small scheduled job closes that gap. Keep a list of signing requests your app considers "pending," and periodically ask the API for their real status:

Since storeSignedDocument overwrites by ID, running it twice for the same document is harmless. That's the property you want from every step in a webhook pipeline: doing it again shouldn't change the result.

None of this is legal advice, but a few facts shape how you build.

In the US, the ESIGN Act and the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (adopted by 49 states) give electronic signatures the same legal standing as handwritten ones for most commercial documents. ESIGN also has requirements around consumer consent and record retention, which is part of why you store the final PDF yourself rather than relying on a third-party link.

In the EU, eIDAS defines three levels: simple (SES), advanced (AdES), and qualified (QES). SES and AdES cover most business contracts. QES requires a qualified trust service provider and certificate-based identity, and some documents (certain property transfers and court filings, depending on the country) require it or exclude e-signatures entirely. Check which level your document types need before you pick a provider, since not every API offers every level.

Across jurisdictions, the evidence that holds up is the same: who signed, how they were identified, when it happened, and proof the document hasn't changed since. That's the audit trail and the completion certificate, which is why Step 6 stores both.

If you're evaluating providers for a workflow like this, the questions that matter at the integration level are mostly not on the pricing page:

The send call is one line. The reliability comes from everything around it: keeping the raw body for verification, checking timestamps and comparing in constant time, acknowledging fast and deduplicating by event ID, downloading files before their links expire, and running a reconciliation job for the events that never arrive. Get those right and contract signing becomes something your app does in the background, with no one chasing signatures or copying PDFs between folders.

For the Firma.dev-specific details used here (event names, header format, rate limits), see the webhooks guide.
